description:
We are a motivated and creative team participating in the NASA Space Apps Challenge. Our goal is to develop an innovative, interactive and visually impressive space-related project.

We are looking for new team members who are passionate about space, science and technology. 

If you are interested in creating something unique, interactive and inspiring, we would love to have you on our team!
summary: Lava Pit Atlas is an interactive map built around one question: could the first base on the Moon or Mars sit inside a lava pit, and where on Earth could we practise it first? We placed 32 pit and skylight candidates on NASA Moon Trek and Mars Trek and gave each one an evidence level (A, B or C), so a void confirmed by radar never looks the same as a guess. For every candidate we compare Earth lava tubes feature by feature: depth-to-diameter ratio, overhang, open skylight and thermal buffering. We show what matches and what does not, and the score gets a confidence band when data is missing. A base ranking and a cost layer then look at local ice, regolith and thermal stability, because every kilogram we do not launch from Earth matters. In our data two sites stand out: the Mare Tranquillitatis pit on the Moon, and the Elysium west-flank candidate on Mars, about 384 km from mapped ground ice.
details:
What it does

Lava Pit Atlas is a web app that maps lava pits and skylights on the Moon and Mars on NASA Moon Trek and Mars Trek imagery. These pits are openings into old lava tubes. A roofed void like that could shield a crew from radiation and micrometeorites, and it smooths out the huge day and night temperature swings: the lunar surface goes above 121 °C by day and down to -133 °C at night, while the shaded floor of the Mare Tranquillitatis pit stays near 17 °C.

The organizers told us they already know the list of analog sites, so we did not make another list. For each Moon or Mars candidate the atlas finds its closest Earth lava tubes and compares them feature by feature: depth-to-diameter ratio, overhang, open skylight and thermal buffering. Each comparison shows what matches, what does not and what is still unknown. Size is never part of the score, because lunar tubes may be 300 to 700 times larger than the ones on Earth and martian tubes up to 80 times larger.

How it works

Every candidate has an evidence letter. A means radar or gravity shows a void, B means imaging or thermal data points to one, and C means shape only, so we do not count it as a base site. No cave on Mars is confirmed yet, and the app says so on every Mars record. Missing values are skipped instead of guessed, and the similarity score comes with a confidence band, so a twin that shares one known feature cannot look as good as one that shares four. The base ranking puts evidence first, then a cost index that counts missing data as zero. A cost page shows why local resources matter: 325 mm of water ice gives the same radiation protection as 975 mm of regolith, and NASA studies show that each kilogram saved on the Mars surface saves 10.5 to 17 kg in low Earth orbit.

We also added layers for lava tube evidence (Mini-RF radar under Mare Tranquillitatis, SELENE radar and GRAIL gravity at Marius Hills, HiRISE at Pavonis and Olympus Mons) and the 1,062 candidates of the Mars Global Cave Candidate Catalog, clearly marked as mostly false positives. Cave Base Mission is a short game on the same data: you run a 10-week mission at a real candidate, and rehearsing at its Earth twin lowers your risk. We label it as a game model, not a prediction.

What we found and why it matters

Two places stood out. On the Moon it is the Mare Tranquillitatis pit: radar evidence of a conduit, 10 to 15 m overhangs, 105 m deep and a stable floor. On Mars it is the Elysium west-flank candidate: an overhanging rim, warmer than its surroundings at night, about 122 m deep and roughly 384 km from mapped ground ice, while the well-known Arsia Mons candidates sit about 2,400 km away. Mission planners can use the atlas to pick where to look next, and the Earth twins tell them where to rehearse first, for example LiDAR and radio tests in Lanzarote, where ESA already trains astronauts.

How we built it

The app is a static website made with TypeScript, Vite and Leaflet, with Python scripts that turn our CSV tables into the matching data. It runs in Turkish and English, works on phones, and has a 60-second tour for first-time visitors. Every number on the site links to its source, and the biggest gap we found is listed openly: the skylight depths of Earth lava tubes are rarely measured. We used Claude (Anthropic) as an AI assistant for coding, research and preparing the slides and demo video. All images are real NASA mission imagery or credited Wikimedia Commons photos, and none of them were generated by AI.
